note: A rectified street-panorama crop of one Amsterdam house front; the house in question fills the middle of the image and neighbours may show at the edges.
source: Questions copied from scripts/jev/run.mjs (lane J1 spike, #326), word form of bays only (the picture form needs five reference images and 5x the tokens); finish drops nothing. Changing any text bumps `version` and so every cache key.
thresholdSource: J1 spike accept rules: gable p>=0.75 (21/21 right, both runs agreeing), finish p>=0.9 (95.2%), bays word p>=0.55 (96.7%), shopfront |noul-0.5|*2>=0.75 i.e. answer probability >= 0.875 (96.7%). One run here, not two: drift was 0-6%.

gable.instructions: What is the shape of the top of the house front in `facade` (the gable or roofline of the main house in the middle of the image)?

criteria.neck: Neck gable (halsgevel): a tall narrow raised centre panel with straight sides, flanked by shoulder pieces or small scrolls, often topped by a small pediment.
criteria.bell: Bell gable (klokgevel): a raised centre whose outline curves like a bell, convex then concave, often with a small arched or rounded top.
criteria.step: Step gable (trapgevel): the outline climbs in stair steps on both sides to a central peak.
criteria.cornice: Cornice or flat top (lijstgevel): the front ends in a horizontal cornice or straight parapet with no raised gable shape; dormers or a roof may show behind it.
criteria.spout: Spout gable (tuitgevel): a narrow pointed or triangular top with a spout-like tip, typical of old warehouses and wooden houses.
criteria.plain: Plain pointed gable (puntgevel): a simple triangular gable following the roof slope, without steps, curves or a neck.

finish.instructions: What is the main wall surface of the house front in `facade` above the ground floor?

criteria.brick: Exposed brick: individual bricks and mortar joints visible in natural red, brown, yellow or dark brick colours.
criteria.painted brick: Painted brick: brick bonding still shows but the whole wall is painted one flat colour (often black, grey, white or dark green).
criteria.plaster: Plaster or render: a smooth rendered surface with no brick joints, usually white, cream or grey.
criteria.stone: Natural stone: the wall is faced in sandstone or other cut stone blocks.
criteria.mixed: Mixed: large parts of the front are clearly different finishes (for example brick with a fully rendered upper storey).

shopfront.instructions: Does the ground floor of the house front in `facade` have a shopfront (large display windows, a shop or cafe front, a fascia or a sign)?

criteria.true: The ground floor is a shop, cafe, bar or other commercial front.
criteria.false: The ground floor is residential: house doors and ordinary windows.

bays.instructions: How many vertical window axes (bays: columns of windows side by side) does the house front in the middle of `facade` have on its upper storeys?

criteria.one: one window axis per upper storey
criteria.two: two window axes per upper storey
criteria.three: three window axes per upper storey
criteria.four: four window axes per upper storey
criteria.five: five window axes per upper storey

gableClassesSource: Spike (Kinkerstraat, 1890s fronts): cornice and step reliable, bell/neck/plain not. Checked on AB07 against the 14 pands that both the register and a confident Jev gable name (H5, 2026-11-10): Jev agreed with the register on 8; its cornice contradicted the register's bell or neck on 5 of 8 calls (3 of them at p>=0.96), so cornice is not written on canal-belt fronts. step and plain are written; bell and neck stay out. Widen only after a buurt of 1890s cornice fronts shows cornice >= 0.9 against hand truth.
